newsitem.title: USA: CME hogs and pork bellies tumble late, end lower.
newsitem.headline: CME hogs and pork bellies tumble late, end lower.

text.p: CME hog and pork belly futures tumbled for sharp losses late and closed lower as long liquidation prompted by concern over cash markets touched off sell stops, traders said.
Hogs finished mostly 1.225 to 0.200 cent per lb lower with April off most at 69.150 cents. Pork bellies ended 1.950 to 0.200 cent a lb lower with May off 1.950 at 75.275 cents.

Unwinding of bull spreads added to early long liquidation and profit taking to trigger sell stops in April late. Concern wholesale pork prices were failing to find expected support weighed on prices, traders said.

"Until we see a series of days at higher money for the cutout and some decent pork movement we will stay away from the buy side" in hog futures, said Dave Maher, livestock analyst with Securities Corporation of Iowa.
The latest CME lean hog index fell $0.40 to $66.96 per cwt.
Adding to pressure was the weak technical picture that developed on the break, they said.
"It sets up a test of recent lows," one trader said.
The recent low in April was set at 68.700 cents a lb which went back to late October.
Rand Financials notably spread long June/short April late. R.J. O'Brien and Lind-Waldock sold April on the early break while ABN Chicogo Corp and Dean Witter sold June, pit sources said.
In hog options, First Chicago continued to spread short April 74 puts and long April 69 puts, pit sources added.

Pork belly futures tumbled late as persistent commerical pressure prompted local liquidation. Concern grew that the CME weekly Out-of-Town Report would show storings last week at the high end of early expectations of 1.0 million to 2.0 million lbs. Sell stops added to the setback, traders said.
After the close, the CME reported a net in-movement last week at out-of-town warehouses of 2.486 million lbs.

Sources noted that although hog slaughter recently had run four percent under a year ago, fresh bellies were moving into storage. This shows a much-weaker-than-year-ago demand for product by end users.
"The demand just isn't there - there's no (bacon) featuring," said Rich Tokheim, president of Investment Research Co.
R.J. O'Brien remained a seller of May late along with Refco. E.D.& F. Man bought at the close, pit sources added.
